title: The Hammer's Road: Herstal to Quierzy
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Herstal, the villa of Pepin on the Meuse
stops.campa: A boy is born in the timber halls above the Meuse, to Alpaida, the concubine of Pepin of Herstal, mayor of the palace and master of all the Franks. The lawful wife's kin will never call him heir; the chronicle calls him what the heirs cannot unmake: elegant, distinguished, uncommonly effective in war. The river runs north past the landing-stages toward Frisia; the boy watches the boats. He is not yet the Hammer. Nothing in Frankland is yet decided.
stops.quote: Charles — an elegant man, distinguished, and effective in battle.
suggested_refs: the Meuse valley of the Pippinids

stops.name: Jupille-sur-Meuse, the deathbed of Pepin of Herstal
stops.campa: Pepin of Herstal dies at Jupille on 16 December, after twenty-seven years as sole master of the Franks. Earlier this same year his legitimate son Grimoald was cut down by an assassin while praying at the shrine of Saint Lambert. The old man's will, held fast by his widow Plectrude, passes the mayoralty over the head of the grown bastard Charles to Grimoald's son Theudoald, a child of six. A dying man's parchment against a living man's sword: the realm holds its breath.
suggested_refs: shrine of Saint Lambert at Liège

stops.name: Cologne, the tower of Plectrude
stops.campa: Plectrude the widow-regent gathers her husband's treasure inside the Roman walls of Cologne and has Charles seized and shut away, lest the concubine's son trouble the child-regency. The stepmother rules Frankland from a strongroom; the future rusts in a cell above the Rhine. The canon does not name his chains, only his patience. Outside, Neustria smells the weakness of a realm governed by a woman and an infant, and begins to arm.
suggested_refs: Plectrude's tomb at St. Maria im Kapitol

stops.name: Forest of Cuise, near Compiègne: the realm cracks
stops.campa: On 26 September the Neustrians rise. In the forest of Cuise by Compiègne they fall upon the boy Theudoald's army and scatter it; the child is carried from the field. They raise Ragenfrid as their own mayor and soon a Merovingian, Chilperic, from a cloister. The Pippinid house that mastered Frankland for a generation is, in one afternoon of hunting-country slaughter, reduced to a widow in a walled city and a prisoner nobody counts. Word of the battle travels down the Rhine to the cell in Cologne.

stops.name: Cologne, the escape
stops.campa: In the confusion of the Neustrian rising, Charles escapes. The canon gives it a hair's breadth and a Hand: with the Lord's help he slips the widow's custody. The chronicle wastes no word on rope or bribe, because the deliverance itself is the fact. A man walks out of a tower in Cologne and into the Ardennes winter, and the Austrasian lords, who want neither the widow, the child, nor the Neustrians, begin to ride to him. The kingless smith has found his forge.

stops.name: The Rhine below Cologne: first battle, and the only defeat
stops.campa: King Radbod of Frisia, ally of the Neustrians, brings his heathen fleet up the Rhine. Charles, with the first raw levy Austrasia gives him, attacks and is beaten, the one defeat of his life, and the canon does not hide it. He loses men and falls back into the hills to learn the lesson every hammer learns: the metal must be heated twice. The Neustrians reach Cologne itself, and Plectrude buys them off with a great part of Pepin's treasure.

stops.name: Amblève (Amel), in the Ardennes
stops.campa: The Neustrians ride home fat with Plectrude's gold, and near Amel on the Amblève Charles falls on them as they rest at midday. He feigns retreat; they break ranks to pursue; he turns and hammers them, the first true hammer-blow, struck against every rule of the old shield-wall decorum, at an hour when Christian armies do not fight. From this day he never loses again. The Ardennes streams carry the news west faster than the survivors can.
suggested_refs: valley of the Amblève at Amel

stops.name: Vincy, near Cambrai (Les Rues-des-Vignes)
stops.campa: On Sunday, 21 March, in Lent, Charles meets King Chilperic II and Ragenfrid in open battle at Vincy near Cambrai. He has offered peace and been refused; now he breaks Neustria's army and chases it to the gates of Paris. Then, in the discipline that marks him, he does not take Paris: he turns his horse east, because the first debt is unpaid. Neustria is broken; Cologne is next. The chronicler sets the day precisely, as one dates the founding of things.

stops.name: Cologne: the treasure yielded, a king raised
stops.campa: Charles enters Cologne not as an escaped prisoner but as the victor of Vincy. Plectrude, the stepmother who jailed him, surrenders the city and what remains of Pepin's treasure; he does her no violence; the canon lets her vanish into a convent's silence. And now the bastard shows he has learned the deepest Frankish art: he raises his own Merovingian, Chlothar IV, a king to sit while he governs. He is mayor of the palace. The kingless years, kings in name, ox-carts and long hair, have begun.
suggested_refs: St. Maria im Kapitol, Cologne (Plectrude's tomb)

stops.name: Soissons, Neustria's last army
stops.campa: Chilperic and Ragenfrid have bought a great ally: Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, comes north with his Gascons. At Soissons Charles shatters the coalition in a single field. Eudo flees across the Loire carrying the king and the royal treasure with him; Ragenfrid runs to Angers. Charles pursues as far as Paris and Orléans, then lets the Loire be a border for now. Every crown-wearing piece on the board is in flight from a man who wears none.

stops.name: The Weser, deep in Saxony
stops.campa: Before the year of Soissons is out, Charles turns the army the other way and drives across the Rhine into Saxony, laying the land waste as far as the banks of the Weser. It is a message written in smoke on both frontiers at once: the house of Pepin is restored, and its reach is the old reach. The chronicler records the river as the measure of the campaign, the way one notches a doorpost to mark a son's height.
suggested_refs: Weser river at the Porta Westfalica

stops.name: Noyon, a king received from the hand of Aquitaine
stops.campa: Chlothar IV, Charles's raised king, dies after his little reign. Charles sends to Eudo; the duke, choosing peace, returns King Chilperic II and the royal treasure across the Loire. And Charles, this is the mercy of the strong, receives as sovereign the very Merovingian he defeated at Vincy and Soissons, and serves him with full honors until the king dies at Noyon within two years. Then a boy, Theuderic, is fetched from the cloister of Chelles. Kings are now grown like orchard stock: chosen, planted, replaced.

stops.name: Utrecht: the death of Radbod, who stepped back from the font
stops.campa: Radbod, king of the Frisians, dies. This is the king who once stood with one foot in the baptismal font and asked Bishop Wulfram where his ancestors were; told they were in hell, he drew his foot back and chose their company. Now he goes to them, and Frisia's gate swings open. Charles takes Utrecht and the lands to the old borders; Willibrord returns to his ruined church and rebuilds; the mission fans out among the terpen and the tidal flats.
stops.quote: I would rather be in hell with my ancestors than in heaven with a handful of beggars.
stops.quote_source: Vita Wulframni (Life of Wulfram of Sens)
suggested_refs: the baptismal font of Radbod in Frisian iconography

stops.name: Geismar, by Fritzlar: the oak of Thunder falls
stops.campa: Under Charles's letter of protection, a sheet of parchment worth an army, the Englishman Boniface takes an axe to the Oak of Thunder at Geismar. The heathen crowd waits for the god to strike him dead; instead a wind from God takes the tree and lays it down in four pieces, in the shape of a cross. From its timber Boniface builds an oratory to Saint Peter. The missionary himself writes it plainly: without the awe of the prince's name, none of this stands.
stops.quote: Without the protection of the prince of the Franks I can neither rule the people of the church nor defend the priests and clerks, the monks and handmaids of God; nor can I forbid the practice of pagan rites and idolatry in Germany without his mandate and the awe of his name.
stops.quote_source: Boniface, letter to Bishop Daniel of Winchester (Epistola 63)

stops.name: The Lippe road into Saxony
stops.campa: Again the Saxons stir, and again the Hammer crosses the Rhine, following the old Roman war-road up the Lippe. The campaign is the rhythm of his reign: spring muster, summer iron, autumn tribute. The chroniclers record these years almost without adjectives: he went, he wasted, he returned victorious, because the repetition is itself the miracle. No mayor before him struck on every frontier of Frankland and was everywhere obeyed.

stops.name: Across the Danube into Bavaria
stops.campa: Charles leads the host over the Danube into Bavaria and bends the duchy of the Agilolfings to his order. He returns with treasure and with a woman of the ducal house: Swanachild, niece of Duke Odilo's line, whom he takes to wife. The marriage is policy braided with desire, and it plants in his own hall the seed of the later quarrel: her son Grifo will trouble the sons of the first bed. The east is fastened; the fastening has a thorn.

stops.name: Alemannia, the upper Danube
stops.campa: Duke Lantfrid of the Alemanni has drifted from obedience; Charles marches into the Swabian uplands and the drift ends. The chronicle notes, with its usual economy, that in this year Lantfrid died, and the duchy thereafter answers to the mayor's writ. Saxony, Frisia, Bavaria, Alemannia: the arc of the forge is complete around the eastern rim. The hammer has made a horseshoe of the Germanies. Now every road in his mind runs south.

segments.name: The Road Between Tours and Poitiers

stops.name: Bordeaux and the Garonne, Eudo overthrown
stops.campa: Abd ar-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus, comes up out of Spain with a great host, crosses the Pyrenees by the western passes, and takes Bordeaux. On the Garonne he meets Duke Eudo of Aquitaine, the victor of Toulouse eleven years before, and destroys his army utterly. The Mozarabic chronicler, watching from the south, gives the slaughter its only possible census. The churches of Aquitaine burn; the host turns north toward the wealth of Saint Martin at Tours.
stops.quote: God alone knows the number of the slain.

stops.name: Quierzy on the Oise, the plea of Eudo
stops.campa: Eudo, who fought Charles at Soissons and made himself a Loire between them ever since, rides north a beggar and stands before his old enemy. The duke who once sheltered runaway kings now pleads for the Frankish sword. Charles hears him, exacts submission, and summons the host of all the Franks: Austrasians, Neustrians, the hardened veterans of fifteen years of forge-work. The canon savors the reversal: pride kneels, and the concubine's son becomes the shield of Christendom.

stops.name: Poitiers, Saint-Hilaire burned
stops.campa: The invaders reach Poitiers and put the basilica of Saint-Hilaire, outside the walls, to the flame. Hilary, hammer of the Arians, watches his roof fall; the city itself holds. Between Poitiers and Tours now lies only the old Roman road and whatever the Franks can put across it, and the treasure-house of Saint Martin, the holiest shrine of Gaul, is the prize the host has named aloud. The relics are the stake; both armies know it.
suggested_refs: shrine of Saint Martin of Tours

stops.name: Moussais, where the Clain meets the Vienne: the seven days
stops.campa: On the road between Tours and Poitiers, by the old town at the meeting of Clain and Vienne, the armies find each other. For seven days they skirmish and probe, each trying to read the other's order. Charles has chosen his ground with a smith's eye: high, wooded at the flanks, narrow enough that horsemen cannot spread. His men are footmen in mail, winter-hard, standing between the riders of the south and everything behind them. Both hosts light their fires and wait for the day.

stops.name: The field of Tours-Poitiers, the wall of ice
stops.campa: On a Saturday in October the horsemen of al-Andalus charge, and the Frankish shield-wall does not move. All day the cavalry breaks on it like sea on a cliff; the chronicler across the Pyrenees fixes the image for a thousand years: a wall, a glacier, and the sword. Toward evening Abd ar-Rahman al-Ghafiqi falls in the press, and the charges die with him. The men of the North stand on their ground in the dark, unbroken, among the dead of two worlds.
stops.quote: The northern peoples remained immobile like a wall, holding together like a glacier in the cold regions. In the blink of an eye, they annihilated the Arabs with the sword.

stops.name: The same field at dawn, the silent tents
stops.campa: At first light the Franks form their wall again and face the enemy camp: the countless tents stand in their ordered streets exactly as before. No horseman comes. Scouts creep forward and find every tent empty: the host of al-Andalus has slipped away in the night, southward, leaving its canvas city and much of its plunder to hold the Franks' eyes. Charles, fearing ambush in the ravines, lets them go. He gathers the spoils and divides them; the chroniclers begin, this same generation, to mint the salvation of Europe from this morning's silence.
suggested_refs: the abandoned tents in Carolingian battle iconography

stops.name: Tours, thanksgiving at Saint Martin's
stops.campa: Charles comes to Tours and stands where the invaders never came: at the tomb of Martin, soldier who cut his cloak in two, patron of the Frankish host. The shrine is unburned; the myth is minted: he is Martellus now, the Hammer, and the clerics write that Christendom itself was the thing defended on that road. Far in the margin of time, an English historian will muse that but for this field the interpretation of the Koran might now be taught in the schools of Oxford; the campa lets the echo stand.
suggested_refs: cappa of Saint Martin (the Frankish palace relic)

stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, the sword left behind the altar
stops.campa: Riding south of Tours, Charles stops at the wayside shrine of Saint Catherine at Fierbois, the tradition holds he founded it, and leaves there a sword marked with five crosses, an offering for the victory, laid up behind the altar for the hand God will one day choose. There it sinks into the earth and the rust of seven hundred years. In 1429 a girl from Domremy, who has never seen it, will send for it by name and place, and the rust will fall away at a touch. The Hammer's road and the Maid's road cross here, at a village altar, across seven centuries.
stops.quote: When I was at Tours or at Chinon, I sent to seek a sword which was in the church of Saint Catherine of Fierbois, behind the altar; and it was found there at once, all covered with rust.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jeanne d'Arc, Trial of Condemnation, 27 February 1431
sources: Procès de condamnation de Jeanne d'Arc (ed. Tisset)

stops.name: Lyon, Burgundy taken in hand
stops.campa: The year after the great battle Charles descends the Saône to Lyon and takes Burgundy in hand, setting his own judges and faithful men over the region as far as Marseille's hinterland. The southern magnates, Roman in their letters and Gothic in their pride, discover what the Saxons learned: the mayor's writ now runs wherever his horses can water. It is administration carried like a campaign: lists, oaths, hostages, the quiet half of the hammer's work.

stops.name: The mouth of the Boarn, Frisia: the temples of the sea-god broken
stops.campa: Charles builds a fleet, the Hammer goes to sea, and sails into the heart of free Frisia, to the mouth of the Boarn. King Poppo brings his boats and his host; the battle goes to the Franks and Poppo is slain. Then Charles breaks the sanctuaries of the heathen gods, the temples of the sea-god among the terpen, and burns them, and carries great spoil home. Where Radbod once drew his foot from the font, the font now comes to Frisia behind the ships.

stops.name: Blaye on the Gironde: the death of Eudo, Aquitaine entered
stops.campa: Duke Eudo dies, and Charles crosses the Loire at once, takes Bordeaux and the fortress of Blaye above the Gironde, and receives the submission of the Aquitanians. He allows Eudo's son Hunald the duchy: on oath, as a grant held of his hand, the new grammar of holding. The old free south learns the case-endings of vassalage. On this rock over the brown water, later ages will say Roland lies buried; the roads of the epics are already being surveyed.
suggested_refs: tomb of Roland tradition at Saint-Romain de Blaye

stops.name: Orléans, the church lands and the canon's grumble
stops.campa: War on every frontier is paid for in land, and Charles takes it where it lies richest: from the Church. Bishop Eucherius of Orléans, who objects, is removed into exile; abbeys and sees are handed to fighting men who owe horses and mail for them: the first knight-fiefs, the seed of a whole world. The canon grumbles and remembers: a holy man is later shown Charles in torment for the plunder of the saints, and his opened tomb at Saint-Denis yields a fleeing dragon and a vault blackened as by fire. Both truths hold: the realm saved, the price entered in heaven's ledger.
suggested_refs: vision of Saint Eucherius (Hincmar, Council of Quierzy 858)
sources: Hincmar of Reims, letter of the Council of Quierzy (858)

stops.name: Avignon, stormed like Jericho
stops.campa: Avignon on its rock has been handed to the Saracens by Maurontus, duke of Provence, and garrisoned against the Franks. Charles sends his brother Childebrand ahead, comes up with the host, and takes the city by storm. The chronicle reaches for Scripture to say how: as at Jericho, with a great shout and the blare of trumpets, over the walls on ropes and engines. The city burns. The Rhone is a Frankish river again, and the army turns down it toward the sea.
stops.quote: In the manner of Jericho, with a great shout and the sound of trumpets, with battering rams and rope ladders they rushed over walls and buildings, and took that fortified city and burned it.

stops.name: Narbonne, the siege on the Aude
stops.campa: Charles crosses into Gothic Septimania and sits down before Narbonne, the Saracen capital north of the Pyrenees, ringing it with lines along the Aude and blockading its garrison under Yusuf. The city that Rome called Narbo Martius holds its walls; the Hammer, who has taken every city he ever touched, cannot starve this one before relief comes by sea. Narbonne will wait twenty-two years for his son. Even in the canon of a saved Europe, one gate stays shut.

stops.name: The river Berre, by the lagoons of Sigean
stops.campa: A relieving army lands from Spain under Omar ibn Chaled and marches for Narbonne. Charles leaves his siege lines and meets it in the valley of the Berre, where the river crawls to the salt lagoons. The Franks break the host; its general falls; the survivors are driven into the marshes and the étang, where men in mail drown among the reeds and the salt-pans, and boats hunt the swimmers. The lagoon country south of Narbonne becomes the canon's image of the sea taking back the invasion.

stops.name: Nîmes, fire in the arena
stops.campa: Marching home, Charles makes Septimania untenable behind him: he wrecks what a garrison could hold. At Nîmes he sets fire to the gates of the Roman amphitheatre, the thousand-year oval the Goths and Saracens had made a fortress; the smoke-blackening on the stones is shown for centuries after. The chronicle lists the ruined towns like hammer-strokes: the method is scorched earth pronounced with Latin precision.
suggested_refs: Arena of Nîmes (fire-marks on the vaults)

stops.name: Béziers and Agde, the walls thrown down
stops.campa: Béziers on its hill and Agde the black basalt port are taken, their walls and citadels demolished, their suburbs burned; Maguelone is razed on its island. No strongpoint is left standing between the Rhone and the lines of Narbonne that a returning fleet could garrison against him. The Hammer's mercy is architectural: he does not massacre these towns, he simply unbuilds them. Behind the army, the coast road smokes from the Rhone to the Pyrenees.

stops.name: Chelles, the empty throne
stops.campa: King Theuderic IV, the boy Charles once fetched from the cloister of Chelles, dies, and Charles raises no successor. The throne of Clovis simply stands empty, and the realm does not fall; the charters begin to be dated by the years of an absent king, and then by the years of Charles himself. It is the boldest act of his life performed as an omission. A kingdom discovers it has been governed by its mayor so long that the crown has become furniture.
sources: Continuations of Fredegar, c. 21 (silence on succession)

stops.name: Marseille and the sea-rocks of Maurontus
stops.campa: Provence rises once more under Duke Maurontus, and Charles comes down the Rhone a second time with Childebrand, and with Lombard king Liutprand as sworn ally at his back. Marseille is taken; the rebellion dissolves; Maurontus flees to a fortress on inaccessible rocks above the sea, and the canon leaves him there, clinging to the last vertical yard of independent Gaul. From the Alps to the two seas, every duke, bishop, and city now holds of the Hammer's hand.

stops.name: Quierzy, the keys of the tomb of Saint Peter
stops.campa: An embassy such as Frankland has never seen comes over the Alps: Pope Gregory III, pressed by the Lombards, sends Charles the keys of the tomb of Saint Peter and a link of the Apostle's chains, begging him to defend Rome: offering to turn Peter from the emperor in Constantinople to the mayor of the Franks. Charles receives the keys with honor, sends Abbot Grimo and Sigebert of Saint-Denis to Rome with gifts, and does not march: Liutprand is his sworn friend, his son's arms-father. The rescue is refused; the door is left open. Through it his sons and grandson will walk to a crown.
stops.quote: He sent to the prince the keys of the venerable tomb and the chains of Saint Peter, with great and countless gifts, such as had never before been seen or heard of.
suggested_refs: chains of Saint Peter (San Pietro in Vincoli)

stops.name: Quierzy, the realm divided like a king's
stops.campa: Feeling his strength ebb, Charles does what only kings had done. With the counsel of his magnates he divides the realm between his sons: Austrasia, Alemannia and Thuringia to Carloman; Neustria, Burgundy and Provence to Pepin, with lordship over Aquitaine and Bavaria at the edges. To Grifo, Swanachild's son, a middle portion that will not hold. There is no king to confirm the act and none is needed; the division itself is the crown he never wore, exercised as plainly as a man dividing his own field.

stops.name: Quierzy on the Oise, the death of the Hammer
stops.campa: At his palace of Quierzy on the Oise, in fever, Charles dies on 22 October 741, aged about fifty-three: mayor of the palace, prince of the Franks, ruler of a kingdom with no king, unbeaten from Amblève to the Berre save once by Radbod's Frisians when he had nothing but his name. The chronicle gives him death in peace: the one engagement he does not choose the ground for. The realm he leaves is not the realm he was jailed in: it is a single forged thing, and it bears his hammer-mark.
suggested_refs: the byname Martellus (first in the 9th-century chronicles)

stops.name: Saint-Denis: a king in all but name, among the kings
stops.campa: They carry him down the Oise and lay him in the abbey of Saint-Denis, among the Merovingian kings, a bastard mayor buried in the royal necropolis, the stone itself pronouncing what the diadem never did. From his body the line runs forward: Pepin crowned within a decade, Charlemagne named for him, the Chanson's Christendom armed in his image. And south of Tours, behind a village altar, a sword with five crosses settles into its seven hundred years of rust, waiting for the girl. The Hammer rests; the iron remembers.
suggested_refs: Basilica of Saint-Denis (later effigy of Charles Martel)
